audits.source_excerpt: Weshparkar, or Veshparkar, was the Sogdian god of the Atmosphere and the Wind. He corresponds to the Avestan god Vayu. In Central Asia, Weshparkar has also been associated to the Indian god Shiva.
audits.retrieval_method: curl of MediaWiki API prop=extracts&explaintext plain-text (titles=Weshparkar; titles=Nanaya with redirects), HTTP 200; raw JSON saved as wiki-weshparkar.json (4173 bytes) and wiki-nanaya.json (32722 bytes) under reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/round5-05/. Direct retry of https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/nana returned HTTP 404 on the restructured site (prior wave: 403), the site's ?s=nana search returned HTTP 403, Britannica returned 403, and no Wayback snapshot of the article exists (availability API and CDX empty), so the prior ledger's blocked target stays blocked; these substitutions are tertiary. CDX capture of sogdians.si.edu (2602 URLs archived) lists the exhibition's image assets 'N2-19-Enthroned-Goddess-E-wall-Temple-II' and 'N4-6-Weshparkar-Detail-Drawing' but no archived HTML text page for either deity.
audits.basis: Partial support, stated exactly, at the level the claim itself states: the two rows' (to-verify) flags are confirmed present verbatim in the baseline entry bytes (prior ledger file 1a1cd3dffe9a9f1ebbe403bcbc32f561f9f5a6147e8fa6e737718075c5629942), and both retrieved passages show the flagged questions are genuinely open rather than settled, which supports the caution and does NOT resolve the flags. Weshparkar: the source gives the spelling variants the row header anticipates ('Weshparkar, or Veshparkar'); a wind/atmosphere portfolio with Avestan Vayu correspondence; a rival derivation 'according to N. N. Negmatov, the inscription Veshparkar is a Sogdian translation of the Sanskrit word Vishvakarman and means "creator of everything"'; Ustrushan and Penjikent image types differing in arm count, heads, and accompaniments; reverence by Manichaeans per B. I. Marshak; and an explicit distinguishability warning — 'It is not always easy to distinguish between the images of such Sogdian gods, strongly Indianized under the influence of Shiva's iconography ... from the images of Shiva himself' — which is the visual-borrowing-is-not-identity caution made by a source, without equating any image with the god's identity. Nanaya: 'her cult spread to various distant locations, including Armenia, Sogdia and Bactria, though it has been pointed out that the goddess in mention was the result of a process of Hellenistic syncretism and it is difficult to tell which of her features had their origin in the Mesopotamian image of Nanaya'; spelling 'always ... "Nanaia" in Greek, but ... "Nana" in Bactrian'; and Panjakent worship to the eighth century of 'a Greek and Kushan-influenced version' whose depictions 'have no clear forerunners in earlier tradition, and appear to be based on four-armed Mahayana Buddhist figures' — a borrowed iconography attached to a name of Mesopotamian derivation, again borrowing without identity. Neither passage mentions the lion or astral attributes, so the entry's specific caution 'not every goddess with a lion is Nana' remains untested here, and the etymology of Wēšparkar (Vayu vs Vishvakarman vs Shiva association) stays contested in the retrieved text itself.
audits.coupling_implication: Myth/era/dress coupling: Sogdian deity identity is a chain of name transmission (Mesopotamian Nanaya → Hellenistic/Kushan → Sogdian Nana; Avestan Vayu / Sanskrit Vishvakarman / Shiva forms for Wēšparkar) whose links date differently, and images are borrowed visual languages, not identity documents. Fictional pantheon or costume work may use the names with dated, region-marked caution but must not merge figures by shared attributes (lion, trident, multiple arms), assign one fixed attribute inventory, or read a Śiva-like figure as 'the same god'.
audits.limits: Both passages are English Wikipedia plain-text extracts — tertiary, editorially unattributed at sentence level, and no open scholarly substitute for the entry's PANTHEON (print), Grenet 2015 (paywalled), or the object publication was reachable this wave (iranicaonline 403/404, Britannica 403, Smithsonian Sogdians site live-403 with no archived HTML text page). The retrieved text does not settle image, attribute inventory, spelling against inscribed attestations, or etymology for either row: all four (to-verify) flags stand, and this audit retires no marker and makes no canon or independent-promotion judgment. The Wikipedia 'Nanaya' article's Sogdian-Nana section and Negmatov's Vishvakarman etymology need primary checking before any upgrade.
